nameStory: Lesser burdock gets its name from being the smaller cousin of greater burdock, though both plants can still grow quite tall! The word 'burdock' comes from 'bur' (those prickly seed heads that stick to everything) and 'dock' (referring to its large leaves). You might also hear it called 'button-bur' or 'cuckoo-button' because of those round, button-like flower heads that later turn into those infamous sticky burs.
description: Lesser burdock is a sturdy biennial plant that can reach 3-5 feet tall, with large heart-shaped leaves and distinctive purple thistle-like flowers. In its first year, it forms a rosette of big leaves close to the ground, then sends up tall branching stems with flowers in its second year. The whole plant has a robust, weedy appearance and is famous for its sticky bur-like seed heads that grab onto clothing and animal fur with tiny hooks.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Round, brown burs about the size of a marble, covered in tiny hooks that grab onto clothing with surprising tenacity - you'll need to pull them off one by one

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Large heart-shaped leaves that can be 6-12 inches long, with a slightly fuzzy underside that feels soft to touch and prominent veining

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small purple thistle-like flowers clustered in round heads, but without the sharp spines of true thistles - safe to touch

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms a flat rosette of leaves in year one, then bolts to 3-5 feet tall in year two with branching stems that spread widely

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Thick, sturdy stems with deep grooves running lengthwise, often with a reddish tinge and slightly fuzzy texture

habitat: Lesser burdock thrives in disturbed soils along roadsides, field edges, vacant lots, and waste areas throughout New England. It particularly loves rich, moist soil and can often be found near barnyards, compost piles, and anywhere the ground has been recently turned over. You'll rarely find it in pristine natural areas - it's a plant that follows human activity.

seasonality.spring: First-year plants emerge as rosettes of large heart-shaped leaves, while second-year plants send up their tall flowering stems. Look for the distinctive fuzzy leaf undersides.
seasonality.summer: Purple flowers bloom from June through August on second-year plants. The round flower heads are clustered at branch tips and attract bees and butterflies.
seasonality.fall: Flowers develop into the notorious sticky burs that ripen to brown and become major hitchhikers on clothing and pets. First-year leaf rosettes remain green.
seasonality.winter: Dried stems persist with empty bur cases still attached, while first-year rosettes may stay green under snow. The sturdy dead stalks are easily recognizable.

funFact: Those annoying burdock burs directly inspired the invention of Velcro! In 1941, Swiss engineer Georges de Mestral examined burdock burs under a microscope after they stuck to his dog's fur during a walk, and the tiny hooks he saw led to his revolutionary fastening system.
confusionNotes: Lesser burdock is often confused with rhubarb when young because both have large heart-shaped leaves, but burdock leaves are fuzzy underneath while rhubarb leaves are smooth. Remember: 'Burdock = bumpy and fuzzy, rhubarb = smooth and edible.'
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'wild rhubarb,' lesser burdock is completely unrelated to garden rhubarb and shouldn't be eaten as a rhubarb substitute. However, the roots are actually edible and are cultivated in Japan as 'gobo,' prized for their crisp texture and earthy flavor.
compareHints: Lesser burdock is smaller overall than greater burdock and has shorter leaf stalks, making the heart-shaped leaves appear to sit closer to the stem. Woolly burdock has much more obvious white fuzz on its leaves and stems, earning its 'woolly' name. Lesser burdock's burs are also smaller and more numerous than those of greater burdock.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Greater burdock is significantly larger than lesser burdock in all aspects - bigger leaves, taller stems, and larger burrs.
Woolly burdock stands out from greater burdock and lesser burdock primarily by its dense white woolly covering that gives leaves and stems a soft, flannel-like texture.
